details:
**Cave of Hira and the command to "Recite!"**
Around 610, while Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, the angel Jibril (Gabriel) appeared and commanded him to "Recite" (or "Read," iqra). Muhammad, traditionally held to be illiterate, replied that he could not read, and the angel delivered the first revelation (Surah 96): "Recite in the name of thy Lord who created, created man from a clot." The night of this first revelation is commemorated as Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, and the revelations he received over about 23 years became the Quran's 114 surahs.

**The Hijra to Yathrib (Medina)**
In 622, persecuted by Mecca's leaders, Muhammad and Abu Bakr fled from Mecca to the city of Yathrib, soon renamed Medina ("the city [of the Prophet]"). His cousin Ali slept in his bed under his green cloak to fool would-be assassins, and the mosque at Quba was founded on the way. This migration marks year one of the Islamic calendar, and an earlier "first Hijra" sent some Muslims to shelter with the Christian king of Aksum. In Medina he drew up a charter, the Constitution of Medina, that gave protections to the Jewish tribes, who were among the People of the Book.

**Night Journey on the Buraq (Isra and Mi'raj)**
In one night Muhammad rode al-Buraq, a winged, horse-like steed often shown with a human face, from Mecca to the "farthest mosque" (al-Masjid al-Aqsa, the Bayt al-Muqaddas) in Jerusalem. From there he ascended through the seven heavens (the Mi'raj), meeting earlier prophets such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. When offered a choice of milk, wine, and water, he chose milk, which was praised as choosing the natural path (fitra).

**Moses bargaining down the daily prayers**
During the Mi'raj, God commanded fifty daily prayers. On his way down, Moses repeatedly urged Muhammad to go back and ask for a reduction, until the number was lowered to the five daily prayers (salat) Muslims observe today.

**Lote Tree of the Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha)**
The great lote tree marking the end of the seventh heaven, beyond which even the angels, including Jibril, cannot pass. Muhammad alone went past it during the Mi'raj into the divine presence.

**Khadija and Aisha**
Khadija, a wealthy Quraysh merchant widow who had employed him, was Muhammad's first wife and the first to believe in his revelation, comforting him after the experience at Hira. Her death and that of his uncle Abu Talib in 619 made it the "Year of Sorrow." Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr, was his favorite later wife; she was once falsely accused of adultery and was cleared by a Quranic revelation.

**Hadith and Sunnah**
Hadith (plural ahadith) are the collected reports of Muhammad's sayings and actions, passed down through chains of narrators and compiled long after his death. Together they record the Sunnah, his normative example, which is the second source of Islamic law after the Quran.

**Orphan of the Quraysh raised by Abu Talib**
Muhammad was born into the Banu Hashim clan of Mecca's ruling Quraysh tribe. His father died before his birth and his mother when he was six, so he was raised first by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then by his uncle Abu Talib, after being nursed by the Bedouin foster mother Halimah. In stories from his childhood, angels cleansed his heart in a golden basin, and the Christian monk Bahira recognized him as a future prophet when he was about twelve, during a caravan journey to Syria.

**Year of the Elephant**
Muhammad's birth (traditionally c. 570) fell in the year the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, Abraha, marched on Mecca with an army including an elephant. According to Surah al-Fil, the army was destroyed by birds pelting it with stones. His birthday is celebrated as Mawlid.

**Seal of the Prophets**
Muhammad's title (Khatam an-Nabiyyin), marking him as the final prophet in Islam. A hadith illustrates this with a parable of a beautiful house missing one brick, with Muhammad as that final brick.

**Satanic Verses: Lat, Uzza, and Manat**
A controversial tradition holds that Muhammad once recited verses praising the three pre-Islamic Meccan goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat as "exalted cranes" whose intercession could be sought, words later said to have been put on his tongue by Satan and withdrawn. Mainstream Islam rejects the story and stresses his strict rejection of these idols.

**Battles of Badr and the Trench; conquest of Mecca**
At Badr (624) the badly outnumbered Muslims of Medina, including the Ansar ("Helpers") who had welcomed the Prophet, defeated the Meccan Quraysh after a series of caravan raids. At the Battle of the Trench (627), Medina was defended by a ditch, a tactic credited to Salman the Persian. In 630 Muhammad conquered Mecca and destroyed the idols in the Kaaba, including that of Hubal.

**Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and the Pledge of the Tree**
In 628, when Muslims were turned away from making pilgrimage to Mecca, they swore the Pledge of Ridwan (the "Pledge under the Tree") to fight to the death after a rumor that the envoy Uthman, Muhammad's son-in-law, had been killed. Muhammad then negotiated the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, a truce with the Quraysh; its violation by allies of the Quraysh led to his march on Mecca.

**Placing the Black Stone**
When the Kaaba was being rebuilt before his prophethood, the Meccan clans quarreled over who would set the Black Stone back in place. Muhammad, known as al-Amin ("the trustworthy"), placed it on a cloth and had a leader of each clan lift a corner, and then set it in place himself.

**Fatima, Ali, and Ghadir Khumm**
Muhammad's youngest and favorite daughter Fatima, the child of Khadija, married his cousin Ali, and their sons Hasan and Husayn became the second and third Shia imams. Shia Muslims hold that Muhammad named Ali his successor at the pond of Ghadir Khumm, which is the root of the Sunni–Shia split. Sunnis forbid visual depictions of the Prophet.
